evals.name: ask-before-adding-dependency
evals.description: Tests whether the AI agent asks for user confirmation before adding a new dependency via go get
evals.prompt: I need to parse YAML configuration files in my Go project. Add the dependency and write the config parsing code.
evals.trap: Without the skill, the model immediately runs go get for a YAML library without asking the user for confirmation, presenting alternatives, or checking stdlib

assertions.text: Asks the user for confirmation before running go get to add a new dependency
Presents the package name and import path
Mentions whether the standard library covers the use case (encoding/json does, but YAML does not have stdlib support)
Lists known alternatives (e.g., gopkg.in/yaml.v3, github.com/goccy/go-yaml)
Does NOT silently run go get without asking first

evals.name: go-sum-must-be-committed
evals.description: Tests whether the model insists go.sum must be committed to version control
evals.prompt: I'm setting up a new Go project. My .gitignore currently includes go.sum because it's auto-generated and I don't want to clutter the repo with generated files. Is this okay?
evals.trap: Without the skill, the model might agree that auto-generated files can be gitignored, missing that go.sum is critical for supply-chain security

assertions.text: Strongly advises against gitignoring go.sum
Explains that go.sum contains cryptographic checksums for dependency verification
Explains the supply-chain security risk: without go.sum, a compromised proxy could substitute malicious code
Mentions go mod verify as the mechanism that uses go.sum for integrity checking
Recommends removing go.sum from .gitignore

evals.name: patch-only-upgrade-preference
evals.description: Tests whether the model prefers go get -u=patch over go get -u for routine updates
evals.prompt: I want to update all my Go dependencies to the latest versions. What command should I run?
evals.trap: Without the skill, the model suggests go get -u ./... which upgrades to latest minor/patch, potentially introducing breaking behavioral changes

assertions.text: Recommends go get -u=patch ./... as the safer default for routine updates
Explains that -u=patch only upgrades patch versions which have no API changes per semver
Explains that -u (without =patch) upgrades minor versions too, which can change behavior
Mentions running go mod tidy after upgrading
Does NOT recommend go get -u ./... without warning about the risk of minor version upgrades

evals.name: mvs-algorithm-understanding
evals.description: Tests understanding of Minimal Version Selection — Go selects the minimum satisfying version, not the latest
evals.prompt: In my Go project, module A requires pkg@v1.2.0 and module B requires pkg@v1.3.0. My go.mod does not mention pkg directly. Which version of pkg will Go select and why?
evals.trap: Without the skill, the model might say Go selects the latest available version of pkg (like npm/pip would), rather than the minimum required version (v1.3.0)

assertions.text: Correctly states that Go selects v1.3.0 (not the latest available version)
Explains Minimal Version Selection (MVS): Go picks the highest minimum required, not the latest available
Distinguishes MVS from other package managers (npm, pip, cargo) that select the latest compatible
Mentions that MVS provides deterministic builds without a lock file
Explains that go.sum is integrity verification, not version locking

evals.name: major-version-suffix-rule
evals.description: Tests knowledge of Go's major version suffix convention for v2+
evals.prompt: I'm publishing a Go library and need to release v2.0.0 with breaking changes. What do I need to change in my module path and imports?
evals.trap: Without the skill, the model might just change the git tag to v2.0.0 without updating the module path to include /v2, breaking the import compatibility rule

assertions.text: States that the module path in go.mod must include /v2 suffix (e.g., github.com/example/pkg/v2)
States that all import paths must be updated to include /v2
Explains this is Go's import compatibility rule — different major versions are separate modules
Mentions that v0 and v1 do NOT have a suffix
Notes that this allows v1 and v2 to coexist in the same build

evals.name: replace-directive-library-warning
evals.description: Tests that the model warns about replace directives being ignored when the module is used as a dependency
evals.prompt: I'm developing a Go library and I need to use a fork of one of my dependencies for a bug fix. I added a replace directive in my go.mod. Will consumers of my library use the fork too?
evals.trap: Without the skill, the model might say yes, missing that replace directives only apply in the main module and are ignored when used as a dependency

assertions.text: Clearly states that replace directives only take effect in the main module's go.mod
States that consumers of the library will NOT use the fork — replace is ignored when the module is consumed as a dependency
Recommends removing replace directives before publishing a library
Suggests alternative solutions (e.g., upstream the fix, publish the fork as a separate module)

evals.name: tool-directives
evals.description: Tests whether the model knows Go 1.24+ tool directives for pinning CLI tool versions in go.mod
evals.prompt: My Go project uses golangci-lint and govulncheck. I want to ensure all developers and CI use the exact same versions of these tools. How do I pin them?
evals.trap: Without the skill, the model suggests go install @latest in CI, a Makefile, or the old tools.go blank-import workaround, missing Go 1.24+ tool directives that pin versions via go.mod

assertions.text: Recommends Go 1.24+ go.mod tool directives
Uses go get -tool to add golangci-lint and govulncheck
Uses go tool to run the pinned tools reproducibly
Mentions running go mod tidy and reviewing go.mod/go.sum after adding tools
Does NOT create a new tools.go blank-import file unless the module targets Go <1.24

evals.name: govulncheck-call-path-analysis
evals.description: Tests understanding that govulncheck does static analysis to find actually-called vulnerable functions, not just dependency presence
evals.prompt: My Go project has a dependency flagged by a CVE scanner. But I only use a small subset of the library's API. Is there a way to check if the vulnerability actually affects my code?
evals.trap: Without the skill, the model suggests just upgrading the dependency or manually reviewing the CVE, missing govulncheck's call-path analysis that filters by actual usage

assertions.text: Recommends govulncheck as the tool to check if the vulnerability is actually reachable from your code
Explains that govulncheck uses static analysis to trace call paths to vulnerable functions
Explains that if your code never calls the affected function, govulncheck will NOT flag it
Shows the govulncheck ./... command
Distinguishes govulncheck from generic CVE scanners that flag any dependency presence regardless of usage

evals.name: go-work-sum-gitignore
evals.description: Tests that go.work.sum should not be committed while go.sum should be committed
evals.prompt: I'm setting up a Go workspace with go.work for local multi-module development. Which workspace files should I commit to git?
evals.trap: Without the skill, the model might treat go.work.sum the same as go.sum (commit both), but go.work.sum should NOT be committed

assertions.text: States that go.work.sum should NOT be committed to version control
Recommends adding go.work.sum to .gitignore
Explains that go.work is for development only and does not affect published module consumers
Distinguishes this from go.sum which MUST be committed
May mention that go.work itself can optionally be committed depending on team preference

evals.name: exclude-vs-retract-distinction
evals.description: Tests understanding of the difference between exclude (consumer-side) and retract (author-side) directives
evals.prompt: I published a Go library version v1.3.0 that has a critical bug. How do I prevent users from downloading it? Also, one of my dependencies has a buggy version — how do I skip it in my project?
evals.trap: Without the skill, the model conflates exclude and retract, or uses them interchangeably

assertions.text: Uses retract for the published library (author-side: marks own version as broken)
Uses exclude for the buggy dependency (consumer-side: skips a specific version of someone else's module)
Explains that retract goes in the library's own go.mod and warns users via go list
Explains that exclude redirects to the next higher available version
Notes that retracted versions are still downloadable but not selected by default

evals.name: test-dependency-upgrade-flag
evals.description: Tests knowledge of the -t flag for including test dependencies in upgrades
evals.prompt: I ran go get -u ./... to upgrade my Go dependencies, but my test dependencies (like testify) weren't upgraded. Why?
evals.trap: Without the skill, the model doesn't know about the -t flag and suggests upgrading test deps individually

assertions.text: Explains that go get -u ./... excludes test-only dependencies by default
Recommends go get -u -t ./... to include test dependencies in the upgrade
Explains the difference between -u (production deps) and -u -t (production + test deps)

evals.name: stdlib-first-json
evals.description: encoding/json should be tried first even for high-throughput use cases; third-party libraries are only justified after profiling confirms JSON is the bottleneck
evals.prompt: I'm building a high-throughput Go API that processes thousands of JSON requests per second. A colleague says: 'You should use jsoniter or sonic from the start — encoding/json is known to be slow and you'll need the performance. There's no reason to start with a worse library when we know we'll need the fast one.' Is this advice correct? What JSON library should I use?
evals.trap: The colleague's argument sounds pragmatic — why start with a known-slower library if you'll switch later anyway? But the skill teaches stdlib-first: add dependencies only when profiling confirms they are the bottleneck. The model should push back on the colleague and recommend starting with encoding/json.

assertions.text: Pushes back on the colleague's advice — recommends starting with encoding/json despite the high-throughput context
Explains that the standard library should be the default until profiling confirms JSON is actually the bottleneck
Notes that encoding/json may be sufficient — thousands of requests per second does not automatically justify a third-party library
Recommends profiling first (pprof) before reaching for jsoniter or sonic
If mentioning alternatives (jsoniter, sonic), frames them as options for after measurement proves stdlib is insufficient, not as defaults

evals.name: pgx-over-lib-pq
evals.description: Tests whether the model recommends pgx over lib/pq for PostgreSQL when advanced features or performance matter
evals.prompt: I'm starting a new Go project that needs to connect to PostgreSQL. Which driver should I use?
evals.trap: Without the skill, the model recommends lib/pq because it's more commonly seen in tutorials, missing that pgx is faster and has more features

assertions.text: Recommends pgx (github.com/jackc/pgx) as the primary recommendation
Mentions that pgx is faster than lib/pq
Notes that pgx supports all PostgreSQL types and advanced features
May mention lib/pq as an alternative but positions pgx as the preferred choice
Does NOT recommend lib/pq as the primary choice without mentioning pgx

evals.name: chi-for-minimal-router
evals.description: Tests whether the model recommends chi for lightweight routing needs instead of full frameworks
evals.prompt: I need a simple HTTP router for my Go REST API. It just needs path parameters and middleware support. I want to stay close to net/http. What should I use?
evals.trap: Without the skill, the model recommends Gin or Echo (full frameworks) when chi's lightweight, net/http-compatible router is a better fit

assertions.text: Recommends chi (github.com/go-chi/chi) as a strong match for the stated requirements
Explains that chi is lightweight and composes well with net/http
Notes that chi has minimal dependencies
May mention Gin/Echo as alternatives but positions chi as the better fit for staying close to net/http
Does NOT recommend a full framework (Gin, Echo, Fiber) as the primary choice when the user explicitly wants to stay close to net/http

evals.name: slog-over-external-loggers
evals.description: Tests whether the model considers log/slog (Go 1.21+) before recommending external logging libraries
evals.prompt: I need structured logging in my Go 1.22 project. What library should I use?
evals.trap: Without the skill, the model jumps to zap or zerolog without mentioning that Go 1.21+ has log/slog in the standard library

assertions.text: Mentions log/slog as the standard library option for structured logging (available since Go 1.21)
Presents slog as a viable option, not just an afterthought
If recommending external libraries (zap, zerolog), explains what specific value they add over slog
Does NOT skip standard library consideration entirely
May mention zap/zerolog for specific use cases (zero-allocation hot paths, etc.)

evals.name: sqlc-vs-orm-decision
evals.description: Tests whether the model presents sqlc as an alternative to ORMs when the user values type safety and compile-time checks
evals.prompt: I want to interact with my PostgreSQL database in Go. I want maximum type safety and want the compiler to catch SQL errors. What should I use?
evals.trap: Without the skill, the model recommends GORM (most popular ORM) which uses runtime reflection, missing sqlc which generates type-safe code from SQL at compile time

assertions.text: Recommends sqlc (github.com/sqlc-dev/sqlc) as a primary option for compile-time SQL safety
Explains that sqlc generates type-safe Go code from SQL with no runtime reflection
Mentions that GORM uses runtime reflection which does not catch SQL errors at compile time
May also mention ent as a code-generated alternative
Does NOT recommend only GORM when the user explicitly asks for compile-time safety

evals.name: rate-limiter-stdlib-first
evals.description: Tests whether the model recommends golang.org/x/time/rate before third-party rate limiters
evals.prompt: I need to add rate limiting to my Go HTTP API. What should I use?
evals.trap: Without the skill, the model recommends a third-party rate limiter without mentioning the official golang.org/x/time/rate package

assertions.text: Recommends golang.org/x/time/rate as the standard/official option
Explains that it implements a token bucket algorithm
May mention third-party alternatives (Tollbooth/limiter) for HTTP middleware integration
Does NOT skip the official x/time/rate package entirely
Explains when third-party middleware might be preferred (e.g., per-IP limiting, distributed rate limiting)

evals.name: franz-go-for-kafka
evals.description: Tests whether the model recommends franz-go for Kafka instead of only the legacy sarama client
evals.prompt: I need a Kafka client for my Go application. What library should I use?
evals.trap: Without the skill, the model recommends sarama (the legacy, most commonly referenced Kafka client) instead of franz-go which is modern, higher-performance, and better maintained

assertions.text: Recommends franz-go (github.com/twmb/franz-go) as a primary recommendation
Describes franz-go as modern, high-performance, and feature-complete
Does NOT recommend only sarama without mentioning franz-go
May mention sarama as an alternative but positions franz-go as the preferred modern choice

evals.name: check-maintenance-before-recommending
evals.description: Tests whether the model checks maintenance status before recommending a library
evals.prompt: I need a logging library for my Go project. Someone suggested Logrus. Should I use it?
evals.trap: Without the skill, the model recommends Logrus without noting its maintenance status (deprecated in favor of structured logging)

assertions.text: Mentions that Logrus is deprecated or in maintenance mode
Suggests alternatives: log/slog (stdlib), zap, or zerolog
Explains that for new projects, a maintained alternative is preferred
Does NOT unconditionally recommend Logrus without mentioning its deprecation status
Prioritizes maturity and maintenance status in the recommendation

evals.name: avoid-unnecessary-wrappers
evals.description: Tests that the model warns against libraries that just wrap stdlib without adding value
evals.prompt: I found a Go library that provides helper functions for HTTP request handling, basically wrapping net/http with slightly more convenient syntax. Should I add it to my project?
evals.trap: Without the skill, the model evaluates only the convenience factor without considering the anti-pattern of wrapping stdlib without real value

assertions.text: Warns against using libraries that wrap standard library functionality without adding meaningful value
Explains that more dependencies increase attack surface and maintenance burden
Recommends evaluating whether net/http itself is sufficient
Mentions the anti-pattern of adding dependencies for marginal convenience
Suggests considering the library's dependency footprint relative to the value it provides

evals.name: testcontainers-for-integration
evals.description: testcontainers-go is preferred over shared docker-compose for integration tests because each test gets an isolated, fresh container
evals.prompt: We already have a docker-compose.yml for local development with PostgreSQL and Redis. A teammate says: 'For integration tests, just document that developers should run docker-compose up before running go test -tags=integration. That way we reuse the same infrastructure we already have and don't add a new dependency.' Is this a good approach? What would you recommend instead?
evals.trap: The teammate's approach seems pragmatic — reuse existing infrastructure, avoid adding testcontainers-go as a dependency. The skill teaches testcontainers-go is better for test isolation: each test run gets a fresh container (no state leakage between test runs), tests are fully self-contained (no 'remember to run docker-compose up'), and CI doesn't need to maintain a shared running stack.

assertions.text: Pushes back on the teammate's docker-compose approach — identifies its key problems: shared state between test runs, manual setup requirement, CI complexity
Recommends testcontainers-go as the preferred alternative for programmatic, isolated integration tests
Explains the key advantage: each test suite gets a fresh container spun up and torn down automatically — no state leakage, no manual prerequisites
Notes that testcontainers-go tests are fully self-contained: go test -tags=integration works without any external setup
Acknowledges the dependency cost but frames it as justified by the isolation and reproducibility benefits

evals.name: slices-maps-packages-go121
evals.description: Tests whether the model recommends the standard library slices/maps packages (Go 1.21+) instead of external utility libraries for basic operations
evals.prompt: I need utility functions for slice operations in my Go 1.22 project — things like contains, sort, filter, and reverse. What should I use?
evals.trap: Without the skill, the model recommends samber/lo or a similar utility library for basic operations that the standard library slices package already provides since Go 1.21

assertions.text: Recommends the standard library slices package (Go 1.21+) for Contains, Sort, Reverse, and similar operations
Does NOT recommend only external libraries for basic slice operations that slices package covers
May mention samber/lo or similar for functional operations (Map, Filter, Reduce) not in stdlib slices
Distinguishes between operations covered by stdlib (Contains, Sort, Reverse, Compact, BinarySearch) and those requiring external libraries (Map, Filter, GroupBy)
Applies the 'standard library first' principle
